summary.text: Marsyas the satyr found the pipes Athena cast away and challenged Apollo to a contest — lyre against flute, with the loser's body at the victor's mercy. Apollo turned his lyre upside down and demanded Marsyas do the same; the satyr could not, and Phoebus flayed him alive until his tears became the river Marsyas in Phrygia.

chapters.title: The pipes
chapters.text: Athena invented the flute but threw it away when Juno and Venus mocked her puffed cheeks in the mirror; she vowed whoever picked it up would be punished. Marsyas son of Oeagrus found the pipes on Ida and grew so skilled that he dared challenge Apollo — they agreed the loser should suffer whatever the winner willed.

chapters.title: The contest
chapters.text: The Muses judged; Marsyas seemed to win until Apollo inverted his lyre and sang while playing — a feat impossible on the flute. Apollodorus says Apollo hung the satyr on a tall pine and stripped off his skin; Ovid tells how Marsyas cried that a flute was not worth his life as living skin was torn from limbs until nerves and viscera lay exposed.

chapters.title: The river
chapters.text: Fauns, satyrs, nymphs, and Olympus his pupil wept; their tears sinking into Phrygian earth became a fountain clear as any spring — the river Marsyas, named for the flayed satyr to this day. Hyginus adds that Midas judged the contest on Tmolus and received ass's ears for preferring Marsyas — a judgment told fully in the tale of Midas.
